desc:
Given a lowercase string s, count the distinct strings that can be made by reordering its letters so that no two adjacent characters are equal. Equal strings are counted once.

Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

s = "aabb"  ->  2   ("abab", "baba")
s = "aab"   ->  1   ("aba")
s = "aaab"  ->  0
s = "abc"   ->  6
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Counting all arrangements and subtracting the bad ones directly is messy because bad pairs overlap. Think of inclusion-exclusion over where equal letters are glued together.

Suppose a letter with c copies is cut into g blocks (compositions of c into g positive parts: C(c-1, g-1) ways). Arranging G blocks in total, where blocks of the same letter are identical, gives G! / ∏ gi! orders.
Forcing blocks to be glued corresponds to the sign (-1)c-g. Multiply, over all letters, the polynomials ∑g (-1)c-g C(c-1, g-1) xg / g!; the answer is ∑G G! · [xG] of the product.
editorial: For one letter occurring c times, call a block a maximal group of copies that were glued together in the inclusion-exclusion. If the copies are glued into exactly g blocks, there are C(c-1, g-1) ways to choose the block sizes, and the sign is (-1)c-g (one factor of -1 for every glue that was used, and c - g glues are used). Then every arrangement of the G = ∑ g blocks, with blocks of equal letters indistinguishable, is counted by G! / ∏ gi!. Summing over all gluings gives exactly the arrangements with no equal neighbours: an arrangement that has equal neighbours is cancelled by the alternating signs.

So the answer is ∑G G! · [xG] ∏letters fc(x) where fc(x) = ∑g=1..c (-1)c-g C(c-1, g-1) xg / g!. Multiply the polynomials one letter at a time (modulo the prime, using inverse factorials) in O(n2) total.

An alternative formulation inserts the letters one by one into the current arrangement while tracking the number of equal adjacent pairs; it reaches the same recurrence with a somewhat heavier state. Brute force over permutations only works up to about 9 letters.
